chapter: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
title: Black patrons, white-owned venues, the mob and numbers
summary: Harlem ballrooms and clubs were patronized but not owned by Black people, with ties to the mob until the numbers game gave some independence; Bill Robinson's political influence.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well, the fact that the Savoy had this color line... Not the Savoy, the Cotton Club. That has been sort of well-known. Then eventually, they moved downtown. But at the same time, there were these other sort of ballrooms going in Harlem -- Small's Paradise was going. And these places were mostly patronized by Black people, weren't they.
But they weren't owned by Black people.

Well, the building wasn't owned by them; the real estate wasn't owned by them. And they had to adhere, a lot of them, to the mob, until they themselves, through the numbers game, became a little monetarily independent, or must stronger -- when they had a much stronger thing to say. Apparently, all things in Harlem didn't point to the political structure. It was either through the church or through the entertainment... Bill Robinson could do more
than a Congressman could do! -- by performing on top of tables for Tammany Hall, you know.
